title: Open the Forecasts screen
prose: I'll highlight Forecasts in the sidebar.
Opening the Forecasts screen.

This is Forecasts. Nothing is computed until you ask for it: choose what kind of forecast you want, the month it should start from and whether it covers one station or the whole network, then press Generate. There is nothing to save or reopen here — a report lives only as long as you leave those three settings alone.
notes: No snapshot, save, version or milestone UI exists in the client. forecastService exposes exactly getStations and generateDemandForecast, and useForecastStore holds a single transient report that is DISCARDED whenever the report type, start month or station changes. Do not write recipes implying a saved forecast.

title: Choose the forecast type
prose: I'll highlight Forecasts in the sidebar.
Opening the Forecasts screen.
These are the two kinds of forecast.

Switching to the ingredient forecast. Provisioning items are the things loaded onto an aircraft — cups, cutlery, bottles. Ingredients are what the kitchen consumes to produce the meals. Changing this discards any report already on screen, because the two are not comparable.
notes: Two radio-style LABEL elements: forecasts.type-provisioning and forecasts.type-ingredient. Switching type clears the current report by design, which is why this recipe stops at the choice instead of generating.

prose: I'll highlight Forecasts in the sidebar.
Opening the Forecasts screen.
Setting the start month to {month}.

The horizon is always twelve months long, so this picks the window rather than its length — starting in {month} means the report runs a year from there. Changing it discards any report already on screen.
notes: Native select of month options, so a fill resolves the visible text ("August 2026"). Verified live: the list starts at July 2026 and the default selection is August 2026.

params.description: Station code or name, or "All stations" for the whole network.

prose: I'll highlight Forecasts in the sidebar.
Opening the Forecasts screen.
Scoping the forecast to {station}.

Each station in the list shows its departure count, which is a useful sanity check on how much data is behind the number — MCT has over 21,000 departures, while some stations have only a handful. "All stations" gives the network-wide picture. Changing this discards any report already on screen.
notes: Native select. Options read like "MCT — Muscat International Airport (21,834 departures)", so a param of just "MCT" resolves by substring. First option is "All stations (network-wide)".

title: Generate a demand forecast
intents: give me the twelve month forecast

steps.message: The report should be on screen before I read it back to you.

prose: I'll highlight Forecasts in the sidebar.
Opening the Forecasts screen.

Generating the forecast. It is computed over every scheduled flight in the horizon, so the wait depends on how much you asked for: a single station came back in a few seconds, the whole network took closer to twenty.
The report is built.
And there it is. The headline figures come first, then the monthly chart, the item-by-item table, the category mix and the written notes.
notes: Verified live: a network-wide provisioning forecast took 18 seconds, a single-station ingredient forecast 3, so the wait carries timeoutMs 60000 rather than the player's 8s default. Two waits on purpose: the generating state first (proof the run started, since a stale report's KPIs would otherwise satisfy the wait instantly), then the assert that the report arrived. It is a read — nothing is persisted.

prose: I'll highlight Forecasts in the sidebar.

Generating the forecast. It is computed over every scheduled flight in the horizon, so the wait depends on how much you asked for: a single station came back in a few seconds, the whole network took closer to twenty.
The report is built.

Five figures across the top. Which five depends on the forecast type: a provisioning report gives you the annual requirement, the peak month, the monthly average, how many items are tracked and the largest category; an ingredient report replaces the last two with the solids and liquids split, in kilograms and litres, since ingredients are not counted in units. Either way the annual figure is the sum of every monthly line in the table below, so the two always agree.
notes: Verified live in BOTH modes. Provisioning, network-wide from August 2026: 68,521,864 units, peak Dec '26 at 7,553,545, average 5.7M, 226 items in 12 categories, largest category Consumables. Ingredient, MCT: 330M kg-equivalent, 285M kg solids, 45M L liquids, peak Aug '26, 187 ingredients in 47 categories. The KPI set genuinely differs between the two, which is why the prose does not name a fixed five.

The mix shows each category's share of the total. Expect it to be lopsided — a handful of high-count consumables usually dwarf everything else by unit volume, which is worth remembering before reading it as a measure of cost or importance. Categories under one percent are shown as "<1%" rather than rounded to nothing.
notes: Verified live: Consumables 73%, Rotable 12%, MINERALS 7%, Alcohol 5%, everything else under 1%. Note the live data also contains a category whose name is a bare numeric string, which shows in the mix as-is — a master-data issue, not a forecast one.

The demand drivers section explains why the shape looks the way it does — how flight volume, route mix and packing standards push the monthly numbers around. Read it before treating a peak as a surprise; usually it is simply where the flights are.
notes: Part of the notes panel. Keep this recipe's prose about causes, and leave the arithmetic to view-executive-summary, so the two are not saying the same thing twice.

title: Read how the forecast was calculated
intents: where do these numbers come from
is this a projection or actuals

steps.message: The report should be on screen before I read it back to you.

prose: I'll highlight Forecasts in the sidebar.
Opening the Forecasts screen.

Generating the forecast. It is computed over every scheduled flight in the horizon, so the wait depends on how much you asked for: a single station came back in a few seconds, the whole network took closer to twenty.
The report is built.

The methodology section is the important one before anyone acts on these numbers. The forecast is not a statistical projection — it materialises each flight's packing standards into per-item manifest lines and sums them by item and departure month across scheduled, non-cancelled flights. So it answers "what does the current schedule imply", and it moves when the schedule or the standards move.
notes: Verified against the report's own text, which describes exactly this aggregation. Worth stating plainly in prose: readers assume "forecast" means a trend projection, and this is a deterministic roll-up of the schedule.

The provenance section states what the report actually drew on. This is the part to check before quoting a number for one station: the station list shows departure counts ranging from tens of thousands down to a single flight, and a forecast built on a handful of departures is arithmetic, not insight.
notes: Part of the notes panel. The departure counts in the station selector are the quickest corroboration of coverage, which is why the prose sends the reader there.

title: Walk through a forecast report
intents: give me a tour of the forecast
i am new to this, explain the forecast
explain each part of the report

steps.message: The report should be on screen before I read it back to you.

prose: I'll highlight Forecasts in the sidebar.
Opening the Forecasts screen.

Generating the forecast. It is computed over every scheduled flight in the horizon, so the wait depends on how much you asked for: a single station came back in a few seconds, the whole network took closer to twenty.
The report is built.
Start at the top: the annual requirement, the peak month, the monthly average, how many items are tracked and the largest category. This is the whole report in five numbers.
The chart is the shape of the year — one bar per month with the peak marked, so you can see where the pressure lands.
The table is the detail behind both: one row per item, one column per month, grouped by category with subtotals and a grand total.
The mix tells you where the volume actually sits. It is normally very lopsided, so read it as volume and not as cost.

And the notes explain the report in words: what it says, what drives it, how it was calculated and what data it rests on. If you only read one part before acting on the numbers, read the methodology — this is a roll-up of the current schedule, not a statistical projection.
notes: The orientation recipe for someone meeting this screen for the first time; it deliberately ends on the methodology caveat rather than on a number.
